Introduction

# VizGenie: Toward Self-Refining, Domain-Aware Workflows for Next-Generation Scientific Visualization

\authororcidAyan Biswas0000-0002-5535-4549    \authororcidTerece L.
Turton0000-0003-4345-7783    \authororcidNishath Rajiv
Ranasinghe0000-0003-3115-1226    \authororcidShawn
Jones0000-0002-4372-870X    \authororcidBradley Love0000-0002-7883-7076

    
\authororcidWilliam Jones0000-0002-3796-6330    \authororcidAric
Hagberg0000-0003-2327-3725    \authororcidHan-Wei
Shen0000-0002-1211-2320    \authororcidNathan
DeBardeleben0000-0002-5593-9205    \authororcidEarl

###### Abstract

We present VizGenie, a self-improving, agentic framework that advances
scientific visualization through large language model (LLM) by
orchestrating of a collection of domain-specific and dynamically
generated modules. Users initially access core functionalities—such as
threshold-based filtering, slice extraction, and statistical
analysis—through pre-existing tools. For tasks beyond this baseline,
VizGenie autonomously employs LLMs to generate new visualization scripts
(e.g., VTK Python code), expanding its capabilities on-demand. Each
generated script undergoes automated backend validation and is
seamlessly integrated upon successful testing, continuously enhancing
the system’s adaptability and robustness. A distinctive feature of
VizGenie is its intuitive natural language interface, allowing users to
issue high-level feature-based queries (e.g., “visualize the skull” or
“highlight tissue boundaries”). The system leverages image-based
analysis and visual question answering (VQA) via fine-tuned vision
models to interpret these queries precisely, bridging domain expertise
and technical implementation. Additionally, users can interactively
query generated visualizations through VQA, facilitating deeper
exploration. Reliability and reproducibility are further strengthened by
Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), providing context-driven responses
while maintaining comprehensive provenance records. Evaluations on
complex volumetric datasets demonstrate significant reductions in
cognitive overhead for iterative visualization tasks. By integrating
curated domain-specific tools with LLM-driven flexibility, VizGenie not
only accelerates insight generation but also establishes a sustainable,
continuously evolving visualization practice. The resulting platform
dynamically learns from user interactions, consistently enhancing
support for feature-centric exploration and reproducible research in
scientific visualization.

###### keywords

Scientific data, Large language models, Agentic workflows, Natural
language, Feature-based visualization.

Scientific visualization is essential for deciphering complex,
high-dimensional datasets encountered across various scientific
disciplines. However, traditional visualization workflows frequently
impose considerable cognitive overhead, requiring extensive manual
intervention, meticulous parameter tuning, and deep domain-specific
expertise. These challenges intensify when dealing with large-scale or
volumetric datasets typical in high-performance computing (HPC)
contexts, where iterative refinement can become exceedingly burdensome.
With ongoing growth in data complexity and volume, there is an urgent
need for intelligent, adaptive visualization systems that effortlessly
translate high-level, feature-oriented queries into meaningful visual
insights, progressively evolving to address new challenges as they
emerge.

Recent developments in natural language interfaces and large language
models (LLMs) offer promising avenues for automating data visualization
processes. Yet existing solutions primarily focus on one-shot code
generation approaches, often needing manual corrections or limiting
users to fixed, predefined functionalities. While some systems
incorporate dynamic code generation and multi-agent orchestration, these
approaches frequently struggle to integrate newly generated modules
seamlessly, systematically validate visual outputs, or adapt flexibly to
domain-specific requirements. Current LLM-driven visualization tools
predominantly handle simpler 2D charting and dashboard generation,
leaving substantial gaps in addressing the complexities inherent in
HPC-scale 3D volume rendering and iterative, domain-specific
exploration. Unlike existing approaches, VizGenie addresses these
critical limitations by integrating robust visual question-answering
(VQA) capabilities, rigorous backend validation, and continuous module
refinement, significantly enhancing reliability and user trust.

A growing body of AI-driven visualization assistants—including
language-to-visualization tools (e.g., Chat2VIS \[[20](#bib.bib20)\],
ChatVis \[[21](#bib.bib21)\], ncNet \[[18](#bib.bib18)\]),
mixed-initiative analytics agents (e.g., LightVA \[[41](#bib.bib41)\],
PhenoFlow \[[13](#bib.bib13)\]), and multi-agent chart refinement
pipelines (e.g., MatPlotAgent \[[39](#bib.bib39)\], VisPath
\[[32](#bib.bib32)\], PlotGen \[[9](#bib.bib9)\])—highlights the
significant potential of LLM-based automation for visualization tasks.
However, the next critical frontier lies in creating self-improving,
domain-aware workflows capable of systematically generating, validating,
refining, and integrating visualization modules in a continuous,
iterative manner. Achieving this requires not only robust code
generation capabilities but also mechanisms to ensure reproducibility,
manage interaction provenance, and efficiently adapt to sophisticated,
evolving visualization needs. Addressing these shortcomings is not
merely incremental but essential, as the complexity and scale of modern
HPC datasets demand visualization tools that minimize user intervention
while maximizing insight generation and reproducibility.

VizGenie, a novel self-improving agentic framework designed explicitly
for adaptive, feature-centric scientific visualization in HPC contexts.
Unlike traditional single-pass visualization systems, VizGenie
orchestrates a seamless integration of stable, preexisting visualization
tools and dynamically generated modules, supported by powerful LLM
orchestration. VizGenie continuously enhances its capabilities through a
structured process of module generation, rigorous validation, and
systematic integration into its visualization repertoire. Users begin
their data exploration with foundational tasks—such as filtering,
slicing, and basic statistical analyses—but can seamlessly transition to
complex, specialized queries that automatically trigger new
visualization module generation.

By leveraging advanced natural language querying and domain-specific
image-based analysis powered by locally fine-tuned vision models,
VizGenie substantially reduces manual overhead. Queries such as
“visualize the skull” or “highlight tissue boundaries” are intuitively
transformed into actionable visualization scripts, eliminating the need
for detailed technical expertise. Users can also interactively query and
analyze the generated visualizations via natural language, leveraging
VizGenie’s VQA capabilities to obtain precise, context-specific
insights. This process is further enhanced through Retrieval-Augmented
Generation (RAG), providing rich, context-driven insights and ensuring
high-quality results. Moreover, VizGenie’s built-in memory
systematically logs prior interactions, queries, and validated
visualizations, facilitating reproducibility and incremental improvement
of the visualization pipeline. By autonomously refining its visual
knowledge base and systematically improving VQA precision, VizGenie
establishes a sustainable and adaptive visualization workflow that
continuously evolves in response to user interactions and data-driven
feedback.

Comprehensive evaluations using complex volumetric datasets demonstrate
VizGenie’s efficacy and adaptability, significantly accelerating insight
generation while establishing new standards for interactive and
iterative scientific visualization workflows. The main contributions of
this paper include:

1.  1.  Agentic Framework Integration: VizGenie uniquely integrates robust,
        domain-specific visualization tools with dynamically generated
        visualization modules, effectively orchestrated by LLMs.
2.  2.  Self-Improving Visualization Pipeline: We introduce a continuous
        cycle of dynamic visualization module generation, validation, and
        integration, allowing the system to progressively adapt and expand
        its capabilities over time.
3.  3.  Feature-Based Natural Language Interface: By combining intuitive
        natural language interaction with image-based feature analysis,
        visual question answering, and retrieval-augmented reasoning,
        VizGenie effectively bridges domain expertise and complex HPC
        visualization tasks, minimizing cognitive overhead.
4.  4.  Rigorous Evaluations and Provenance: We provide extensive
        experimental results demonstrating VizGenie’s effectiveness on
        real-world scientific datasets, underscoring substantial
        improvements in efficiency, reproducibility, and domain-specific
        visualization accuracy.

## 1 Related Work

The goal of automating data visualization has a long history e.g.
\[[19](#bib.bib19), [11](#bib.bib11)\]. Recently, the advent of AI/ML
and natural language interfaces (NLI) has resulted in new ways to
automate the visualization process. The success of applying NLI and LLM
approaches for automated visualization in information visualization
strongly motivates using those capabilities for large-scale scientific
data visualization, including simulation data produced by
supercomputers.

Scientific data, particularly large-scale simulation data or other 3D
data, presents special challenges for automating the visualization
process. The features and regions of interest are often amorphous
objects that shift and change as the view angle changes. The language
used to describe the scientifically interesting features is
domain-specific jargon that may be quite different from the natural
language on which large language models are trained. Scientific data is
often multi-dimensional, temporal, highly evolving, and needs
specialized visualization applications \[[6](#bib.bib6), [1](#bib.bib1),
[14](#bib.bib14)\] and data structures \[[30](#bib.bib30),
[10](#bib.bib10)\]. For 3D simulation data, the important features may
span multiple variables or data types. The appropriateness of different
volume visualization techniques \[[3](#bib.bib3), [27](#bib.bib27),
[38](#bib.bib38)\] varies depending on data, compute resources or
visualization goals. Techniques such as streamlining or lighting can be
used to highlight specific features or emphasize temporal change. Color
mapping choices and techniques can be used to accentuate features.

There is limited research in automating visualizations for scientific
data, particularly large-scale HPC-derived simulation data. ChatVis
\[[21](#bib.bib21)\] is used to develop ParaView \[[1](#bib.bib1)\]
Python scripts in an iterative LLM-based workflow that includes a
feedback loop that takes resultant error messages and inputs them back
into the LLM until the script can correctly generate the requested
visualization. VizGenie builds upon recent approaches like ChatVis,
which also employs LLM-based workflows for scientific visualization.
ChatVis focuses primarily on iterative generation and debugging of
ParaView scripts through natural language prompts. In contrast, VizGenie
expands significantly on this paradigm by integrating domain-aware,
feature-centric querying, VQA via fine-tuned vision models, and
continuous self-refinement alongside RAG capabilities. Additionally,
VizGenie orchestrates a broader array of dynamically generated modules
beyond simple scripting, systematically validating and integrating these
modules into an evolving agentic workflow.

![Refer to caption](2507.21124v1/figs/system_overview_Images.png)

Figure 1: An example of feature-based interactions of a user with
VizGenie for CT scan data set. Users can make open-ended natural

are not specified.

Many LLM-based information visualization workflows have informed this
work. Vega \[[29](#bib.bib29)\] and Vega-lite \[[28](#bib.bib28)\]
introduced a data flow architecture and a high-level grammar for
graphics, encodings, and composing to generate automatic visualizations.
NcNet \[[18](#bib.bib18)\] uses a transformer model to go from query to
visualization. By including the capability of one-shot hints or
iterative conversation to improve end results, ncNet foreshadows an
agentic approach. Chat2VIS \[[20](#bib.bib20)\] explored the efficacy of
several LLMs combined with prompt engineering to produce more effective
visualizations. FREYR \[[8](#bib.bib8)\] introduces a framework that
breaks down tool usage into separate steps to achieve better
performance. LM4HPC \[[5](#bib.bib5)\] provides a framework for HPC
related tasks such as code analysis and optimization. A wide range of
approaches can be found in the survey literature \[[2](#bib.bib2),
[33](#bib.bib33)\].

The field of human-AI collaboration in visual analytics is growing. In
this collaborative approach, users interactively guide and modify the
visualization process. This research highlights the benefits of
integrating natural language interfaces with traditional visualization
tools to reduce cognitive overhead and improve overall usability. Recent
examples include LightVA \[[41](#bib.bib41)\] and PhenoFlow
\[[13](#bib.bib13)\]. LightVA develops a framework with an agent
workflow for task planning and execution. PhenoFlow creates a
domain-specific framework to support visual analytics in the medical
field of stroke management. An LLM is used as the data wrangler while
the NLI supports the medical expert to interact with visual analytics.

![Refer to caption](2507.21124v1/figs/workflow_updated.png)

Figure 2: A schematic diagram of our proposed workflow.

Research such as VisPath \[[32](#bib.bib32)\] and PlotGen
\[[9](#bib.bib9)\] employs multi-agent or ensemble approaches to
generate, validate, and refine visualization outputs. These works
emphasize coordinated agents that handle different sub tasks (e.g.,
planning, code generation, and feedback) and demonstrate the benefits of
diverse reasoning paths for robust visualization synthesis. Both VisPath
and PlotGen leverage MatPlotBench \[[39](#bib.bib39)\] for validation.
Finding adequate benchmarks is a challenge for automated scientific
visualization systems. Two commonly used ones for information
visualization, MatPlotBench and NVBench \[[17](#bib.bib17)\], offer
standardized datasets but those datasets and visualizations are geared
towards typical information visualization tasks (e.g., bar charts,
histograms, etc). Both benchmarks include sets of example
visualizations. However, these are primarily 2D plots that do not
include the large scale scientific data of the type targeted by
VizGenie.

Several studies incorporate mechanisms for automatic validation, error
detection, and iterative improvement of generated visualization modules.
These papers address the challenges of maintaining reproducibility and
adapting to new data or evolving user requirements, providing a contrast
to approaches that rely solely on one-time code generation. HaiChart
\[[37](#bib.bib37)\], used Reinforcement learning (RL) framework to
iteratively refine and generate high-quality data visualizations using a
Monte Carlo Graph Search algorithm \[[15](#bib.bib15)\], composite
reward function, and user feedback, outperforming both human-powered and
other AI-powered tools. On the other hand, ShiftScope
\[[26](#bib.bib26)\] uses two actor-critic agents based on the PPO
algorithm \[[31](#bib.bib31)\] to interactively adapts to users’
evolving data focus by learning to recommend personalized and relevant
visualizations.

Pre-trained vision language models (VLM) such as Llava
\[[16](#bib.bib16)\], Llama-3.2-vision, Qwen2-VL \[[34](#bib.bib34)\]
models can be efficiently fine tuned to adopt for domain specific
sciences and use cases using data centralized implementation applying
Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA \[[12](#bib.bib12)\]) and in federated
learning settings using Flora \[[22](#bib.bib22)\]. LoRA introduces
trainable low-rank matrices into the attention projection layers
(specifically targeting the query, key, and value matrices), thereby
drastically reducing the number of parameters that require updating,
reducing computational cost and risk of overfitting while training with
small data sets.

## 2 System Requirements

To effectively address the challenges in modern scientific visualization
workflows, particularly for complex and large-scale high-performance
computing (HPC) data, we identify the following key requirements:

R1. Natural Language Interaction:  
The system must interpret high-level, domain-specific queries in natural
language to reduce cognitive load and bridge the gap between domain
expertise and technical visualization implementation.

R2. Dynamic Extensibility:  
Visualization needs evolve continually; thus, the system must
autonomously extend its capabilities through dynamic generation,
validation, and integration of new visualization modules.

R3. Domain-Aware Visualization:  
The system should leverage domain-specific knowledge to automatically
identify and visualize scientifically relevant features, avoiding
generic, non-specific interpretations.

R4. Reproducibility and Provenance:  
It is essential to systematically track and log interactions,
visualizations, and decisions made by the system to ensure
reproducibility and traceability of scientific findings.

R5. Robustness and Error Handling:  
Generated modules must undergo validation, including automatic detection
and iterative correction of errors, to maintain robustness and
reliability in diverse scientific scenarios.

R6. Responsive User Interface:  
The system must offer an intuitive and interactive user interface that
clearly presents visualization outputs, intermediate reasoning steps,
and actionable suggestions to facilitate efficient exploration and
iterative refinement.

These requirements set the foundational objectives for our VizGenie
system, guiding its design and implementation toward delivering a
next-generation visualization experience for scientific research.

## 3 System Overview

VizGenie is specifically designed to address the requirements, Sec.
[2](#S2 "2 System Requirements ‣ VizGenie: Toward Self-Refining, Domain-Aware Workflows for Next-Generation Scientific Visualization"),
providing researchers with an intuitive and adaptive visualization
experience. Users interact with VizGenie by simply pointing to a
directory containing multiple simulation files. They can then pose
natural language questions such as _"How many datasets are available?"_,
_"What are the characteristics of this simulation run?"_, or more
complex feature-based queries such as _"Where does this specific feature
occur across simulations?"_ or _"Can you visualize the boundaries of the
region of interest?"_. These queries are effortlessly translated by
VizGenie into actionable tasks. Figure
[1](#S1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 1 Related Work ‣ VizGenie: Toward Self-Refining, Domain-Aware Workflows for Next-Generation Scientific Visualization")
illustrates an example interaction, highlighting the system’s response
to feature-based user queries.

At its core, VizGenie integrates specialized, domain-specific
visualization modules alongside dynamically generated components (R2,
R3). Users can initiate data exploration by requesting statistical
analyses, extracting informative slices, or filtering datasets based on
custom thresholds. As queries evolve, the system leverages LLMs to
dynamically generate new visualization scripts—such as volumetric
rendering via VTK \[[30](#bib.bib30)\], specialized feature
highlighting, or iterative refinement of existing visualizations—thereby
continuously expanding its capabilities.

The intelligent, agentic workflow of VizGenie is a critical innovation,
automating routine visualization tasks while enabling advanced,
domain-specific feature extraction and visualization. Complex queries
trigger coordinated processes where the system retrieves, analyzes, and
visualizes data using tailored, validated techniques (R5). Rigorous
validation ensures generated outputs are robust, and successful modules
are seamlessly integrated into the existing visualization repertoire,
enabling continuous system refinement and evolution.

By combining natural language processing (R1), dynamic module
generation, and specialized image-space analysis using vision models,
VizGenie significantly reduces cognitive overhead (R6). It empowers
users to concentrate on insights and discoveries rather than manual
configuration and technical implementation details. The following
sections detail how VizGenie’s innovative design, iterative validation
mechanisms, and responsive user interface collectively establish a new
standard for adaptive, feature-centric scientific visualization
workflows. A schematic representation of the workflow is presented in
Figure
[2](#S1.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 1 Related Work ‣ VizGenie: Toward Self-Refining, Domain-Aware Workflows for Next-Generation Scientific Visualization").

## 4 Methodology and System Design

The design of VizGenie directly addresses the system requirements
outlined in Sec.
[2](#S2 "2 System Requirements ‣ VizGenie: Toward Self-Refining, Domain-Aware Workflows for Next-Generation Scientific Visualization").
The following subsections detail our methodological innovations and
system components that collectively enable our sophisticated, adaptive
visualization workflow.

### 4.1 Background and Motivation: Automated Agentic Workflows via User Specifications

In the context of automated AI workflows, an agent\[[36](#bib.bib36)\]
can be described as a model-driven orchestrator that combines internal
reasoning traces with explicit externally grounded actions. An LLM-based
agent can maintain a dynamic context of thoughts, invoke tools or
functional APIs, and adapt its strategy based on intermediate results
(e.g., using ReAct paradigm \[[40](#bib.bib40)\]). Building on a single
agent’s ability to utilize multiple tools, a multi-agentic system forms
a coordinated ensemble of agents– each with its own state, expertise and
sub task focus. These agents can communicate with each other, negotiate
or delegate responsibilities, and collaboratively decompose and solve
user provided goals.

Such agentic workflows can offer a far greater flexibility and
robustness than static, rule-based automation approaches.

Inspired by recent advancements in automated agentic systems, we
initially developed a purely automated agentic workflow where LLM-based
agents dynamically generated and executed code based solely on natural
language instructions. In this multi-agent workflow: Agent 1, the
orchestrator-planner, transforms the user specification into concrete
tasks, coordinates their execution, and evaluates intermediate results;
Agent 2, the code generator-executor, iteratively produces, runs, and
refines code or system commands to meet those tasks; and Agent 3, the
security sentinel, scrutinizes every proposed snippet and command for
harmful patterns, data exfiltration, or operations outside the permitted
environment. To further contain security risks from LLM-based automated
workflows, we combined OS isolation with LLM policy filtering. Every
agent-generated Python program ran on a network-connected laptop in a
single fresh, non-privileged account whose access was confined to a
single experiment directory, blocking any change to system files or
other users’ data.

By clearly separating planning, implementation, and protection, this
orchestrator–executor–sentinel loop provided flexible, just-in-time
visualization generation without pre-installed software dependencies.
However, we quickly observed limitations: relying exclusively on
dynamically generated software was computationally inefficient and
inconsistent, with roughly half the trials yielding successful outcomes
(i.e., generated code executed properly and produced visualizations as
per users’ specifications). These challenges prompted our development of
the hybrid VizGenie system where dynamic module generation and execution
is coupled with _pre-existing_ tools and the system goes through
self-improvement cycles independent of user interactions.

### 4.2 VizGenie: Visualization-aware Agentic Workflow

VizGenie integrates stable, predefined visualization modules with the
flexibility of dynamic module generation via LLMs. Its natural language
interface supports iterative refinement, continuous learning, and
domain-specific visualization tailored to evolving scientific needs.

#### 4.2.1 Agent Architecture and Tool Selection

VizGenie’s workflow incorporates a single LLM-agent with multiple tools.
The tools are selected by the LLM agent using
zero-shot-react-description. The set of tools can be categorized into
two classes: 1) pre-existing (e.g., FilterRuns, VisualizeHistogram,
VisualizeHistogram), and 2) dynamic LLM-generated (e.g., SimulationInfo,
CodeGenerator, ModifyGeneratedCode, LookupFeatureInDataset).
Pre-existing tools enable faster execution and more reliable outcomes.
LLM-generated modules are dynamically generated when user queries exceed
pre-existing list of capabilties (more details in Section
[4.2.3](#S4.SS2.SSS3 "4.2.3 Balanced Use of Pre-existing and Dynamic Modules ‣ 4.2 VizGenie: Visualization-aware Agentic Workflow ‣ 4 Methodology and System Design ‣ VizGenie: Toward Self-Refining, Domain-Aware Workflows for Next-Generation Scientific Visualization")).

We strategically employ specialized LLMs for distinct phases of our
VizGenie workflow—covering both agentic orchestration and the on-the-fly
generation of new modules:

- •
  Workflow Orchestration: A deterministic instance of GPT-4o ensures
  reliable high-level coordination.
- •
  Code Generation: Creative and exploratory code generation is handled
  by o3-mini with higher temperature settings (temperature=1).
- •
  Incremental Code Refinement: For precise modifications, we deploy
  GPT-4o-mini with deterministic settings to avoid introducing
  unintended variability and improve response time.
- •
  General Text Analysis and Q&A: General text-based user interactions to
  handle Q&A regarding data sets and feature-queries, we deploy GPT-4o
  for stability and reasonable response time.

For code generation and modification related tasks, we provide a set of
predefined requirements (e.g., "Generate valid Python code that uses the
VTK library to visualize data.", "The module must define a function
named update_vtk_scene(renderer) that takes a VTK renderer as input and
updates it.") and the LLM-agent extracts user-defined specifications
(prompt) from the chat interactions and overrides the predefined specs
("Must Implement these functionalities, overriding the defaults:
prompt").

#### 4.2.2 Contextualized Data Queries

VizGenie incorporates context-aware querying through its Simulation Info
tool that provides general information about the available data sets. By
parsing directory structures of the data folder (that has all the data
files inside it) and optional user-provided metadata (e.g., README
files), the system constructs context-driven prompts based on user
queries. These enable the LLM to respond precisely and
domain-specifically to question such as "how many data sets do I have?"
or "tell me more about xyz.vti data set", significantly enhancing query
relevance and reducing ambiguity in exploratory workflows.

#### 4.2.3 Balanced Use of Pre-existing and Dynamic Modules

VizGenie combines robust, validated tools (e.g., FilterRuns,
VisualizeRun, AnalyzeRuns) with dynamically generated visualization
modules created via the CodeGenerator tool. When user queries exceed
baseline capabilities, the system autonomously synthesizes new VTK
Python scripts using LLMs and logs them in a SQLite database that gets
validated (details in Section
[4.2.5](#S4.SS2.SSS5 "4.2.5 Validation and Iterative Error Correction ‣ 4.2 VizGenie: Visualization-aware Agentic Workflow ‣ 4 Methodology and System Design ‣ VizGenie: Toward Self-Refining, Domain-Aware Workflows for Next-Generation Scientific Visualization"))
for future use. This database acts like a cache that is later looked up
by the agent to find modules that match user requirements before it
decides to generate new code. This design ensures both stability and
adaptability, meeting evolving visualization demands without
compromising reliability.

#### 4.2.4 Optimizing Code Generation: Full Regeneration versus Incremental Updates

To optimize computational efficiency and maintain robustness, VizGenie
employs a dual strategy for code generation:

- •
  Full Regeneration: Triggered for entirely new visualization scenarios,
  ensuring tailored solutions from scratch.
- •
  Incremental Updates: Employed for minor adjustments (e.g., color
  mapping, opacity tuning), minimizing redundancy and preserving
  validated code integrity.

This approach balances flexibility with operational efficiency,
significantly reducing error introduction risks.

#### 4.2.5 Validation and Iterative Error Correction

To ensure visualization module reliability, VizGenie includes
comprehensive validation and iterative correction phases. Newly
generated code modules undergo automated execution testing, capturing
runtime outputs and errors. Identified issues trigger iterative
refinement through targeted LLM prompts until achieving error-free
operation or reaching predefined iteration limits. Validated modules are
integrated into a persistent cache, ensuring reproducibility and
maintaining robust operational standards. To optimize the response time,
our experiment shows that o3-mini produces the best results compared to
the other LLMs (such as GPT-4o), reducing the need for iterative
evaluation. For ensuring that all the user specifications are included
in the code, we perform the full validation via asynchronous
self-improvement (Section
[4.2.7](#S4.SS2.SSS7 "4.2.7 Continuous, Asynchronous Self-Improvement ‣ 4.2 VizGenie: Visualization-aware Agentic Workflow ‣ 4 Methodology and System Design ‣ VizGenie: Toward Self-Refining, Domain-Aware Workflows for Next-Generation Scientific Visualization")).

![Refer to caption](2507.21124v1/figs/finetuning_workflow2.png)

Figure 3: A schematic depiction of our fine-tuning workflow for
domain-specific adaptation of vision models with Deep Water Impact data
set. Images are either drawn from \[[24](#bib.bib24)\] or

#### 4.2.6 Advanced Feature-based Query Handling Using Domain-Specific Fine-tuning of Llama-Vision Models

A core innovation of VizGenie is its sophisticated support for
feature-based queries, leveraging a locally fine-tuned Llama-Vision
model. The system automates image-based analysis of dataset
visualizations, extracting meaningful feature descriptions stored in a
structured knowledge base. These metadata significantly improve accuracy
in determining optimal visualization parameters (e.g., isovalues) via
intelligent, LLM-driven aggregation and reasoning (Figure
[3](#S4.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 4.2.5 Validation and Iterative Error Correction ‣ 4.2 VizGenie: Visualization-aware Agentic Workflow ‣ 4 Methodology and System Design ‣ VizGenie: Toward Self-Refining, Domain-Aware Workflows for Next-Generation Scientific Visualization")).
Given a data set and a (fine-tuned) vision model, we generate a
collection of images for varying camera angles and iso-values that are
then used for generating captions via the vision model. These captions,
along with the isovalues and data set identifiers are stored in a
database. This database is used by the agent to retrieve the most
relevant isovalue given the user’s query for a given data set, and is
visualized. An LLM (GPT-4o) is used to decide the best matching isovalue
given the caption descriptions.

To accurately support domain-specific queries and enhance the vision
model’s understanding of scientific visualization contexts, we
implemented a targeted fine-tuning strategy for our locally deployed
Llama-Vision model. This fine-tuning process ensures that feature-based
queries and VQA outputs are accurate and directly relevant to complex
visualization scenarios encountered in scientific exploration.

##### Dataset Generation:

We began by systematically generating a representative dataset
consisting of screenshots from multiple camera angles and varying
visualization parameters (e.g., isovalues, volume renderings with
different opacity settings and background colors, etc) for each dataset
under consideration. In order to test fine-tuning with domain-specific
knowledge, we targeted the Deep Water Impact asteroid data Fig.
[3](#S4.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 4.2.5 Validation and Iterative Error Correction ‣ 4.2 VizGenie: Visualization-aware Agentic Workflow ‣ 4 Methodology and System Design ‣ VizGenie: Toward Self-Refining, Domain-Aware Workflows for Next-Generation Scientific Visualization")
with additional images curated from the data release documentation
\[[24](#bib.bib24)\] and additional visualizations generated from
ParaView. The isosurface images ($`\approx`$ 50 in total) and curated
images were accompanied by carefully constructed annotations describing
the primary visual features, characteristics, and scientifically
relevant observations. One of the authors, a visualization scientist
with domain relevant experience, curated, generated, reviewed and
refined these image-caption pairs, ensuring their accuracy and
relevance.

##### Annotation, Quality Control and Fine-Tuning:

Each caption was carefully designed to succinctly describe key visual
features, including specific domain terminology and context-specific
observations. A quality assurance process involving manual reviews by
the relevant expert ensured high-quality annotations, minimizing
ambiguity and maximizing the dataset’s value for fine-tuning. Next, we
utilized parameter-efficient Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA)
\[[12](#bib.bib12)\] to fine-tune the Llama-Vision model (v3.2 with 11
billion parameters) on a NVIDIA A100-PCIE-40GB GPU. More details
regarding the fine-tuning procedure is available in supplemental
material.

##### Integration and Evaluation:

Post-fine-tuning, the enhanced Llama-Vision model was seamlessly
integrated back into VizGenie’s workflow. To validate effectiveness, we
assessed the accuracy of VQA results on held-out test images and
qualitatively examined improvements in the precision of feature
descriptions and recommended visualization parameters (e.g., optimal
isovalues). Results demonstrated substantial gains in both descriptive
accuracy and domain-specific relevance, directly benefiting users in
feature-driven explorations. More details about quality analysis are
shown in Section
[12](#S6.F12 "Figure 12 ‣ 6 Case Study ‣ VizGenie: Toward Self-Refining, Domain-Aware Workflows for Next-Generation Scientific Visualization").

This targeted domain-specific fine-tuning approach significantly
improves the overall capability and reliability of VizGenie’s
feature-based query system, enabling context-aware visualization for
complex scientific datasets.

#### 4.2.7 Continuous, Asynchronous Self-Improvement

VizGenie employs autonomous, asynchronous refinement mechanisms
independent of direct user interaction:

- •
  Improve Toolset: Periodic validation cycles proactively ensure newly
  generated modules are error-free and ready for future interactions.
- •
  Improve VQA Capabilities: Iterative screenshot analyses refine the
  underlying knowledge base by identifying and incorporating previously
  unseen features and metadata.

These self-improvement strategies collectively sustain the system’s
adaptability, responsiveness, and domain relevance.

#### 4.2.8 Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Contextual Refinement

To enhance contextual understanding during question/answer sessions,
VizGenie implements a lightweight RAG mechanism. By retrieving relevant
historical interactions and utilizing domain specific research via
locally stored documents, RAG enriches the LLM’s contextual awareness,
facilitating more accurate default parameter suggestions and improved
code quality, particularly when user guidance is minimal. This method
elevates the system’s usability and domain adaptability.

Collectively, these methodological innovations establish VizGenie as a
robust, adaptive visualization platform that systematically addresses
the identified system requirements, setting new benchmarks in agentic
scientific visualization workflows.

## 5 Interface Design

![Refer to caption](2507.21124v1/figs/interface_design3.png)

Figure 4: Screenshot of VizGenie’s chat and visualization interface.

The VizGenie interface is carefully designed to embody and directly
support the system requirements in Sec.
[2](#S2 "2 System Requirements ‣ VizGenie: Toward Self-Refining, Domain-Aware Workflows for Next-Generation Scientific Visualization"),
providing an intuitive, transparent, and interactive user experience.
Developed using PyQt5, the interface integrates various system
components seamlessly, enhancing user engagement, reducing cognitive
overhead, and ensuring robust domain-specific visualization. Figure
[4](#S5.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 5 Interface Design ‣ VizGenie: Toward Self-Refining, Domain-Aware Workflows for Next-Generation Scientific Visualization")
illustrates our interactive chat-based user interface, demonstrating how
it cohesively supports advanced agentic workflows. The interface has
four main sections: a user/agent chat panel; an agent reasoning panel; a
2D image display panel; and a 3D VTK visualization rendering panel. The
interface supports interactive callbacks and follow-up suggestions while
integrating validation feedback. Details on the interface are in the
supplemental material.

## 6 Case Study

All experiments with VizGenie were conducted on a Macbook Pro with M3
chip that has 128GB Memory and 2TB of storage. For our initial case
study, we have added four different datasets:

1.  1.  A CT scan dataset \[[7](#bib.bib7)\]; this dataset is downloaded
        with ParaView \[[1](#bib.bib1)\] as part of its example data.
        Originally produced by Siemens Medical Systems, it is a CT study of
        the head of a twelve year old male with a hole in the skull near the
        left side of the nose. The volume rendering includes the head and
        neck from just above the eyes to just below the chin.
2.  2.  Hurricane Isabel dataset from the 2004 SciVis contest
        \[[35](#bib.bib35)\]; This dataset contains thirteen variables with
        a resolution of $`500\times 500\times 100`$ for each time step. For
        our experiments, we have chosen to work with time step 25 and with
        the pressure field and use subsampled resolution of
        $`250\times 250\times 50`$.
3.  3.  Astrophysics Turbulence Simulation Data from 2008 SciVis contest
        \[[23](#bib.bib23)\]; this data set explores how instabilities in an
        ionization front related to the formation of the universe’s first
        stars. It contains measurements of the relative abundances of eight
        chemical species, along with temperature, density, and the velocity
        field. The data is structured at a resolution of
        $`600\times 248\times 248`$ per time step, and we have selected time
        step 99 for our analysis, focusing on the temperature variable.
4.  4.  Deep Water Asteroid Impact dataset from 2018 SciVis contest
        \[[24](#bib.bib24)\]; The Deep Water Impact Ensemble dataset is
        derived from a series of simulations conducted at Los Alamos
        National Laboratory to investigate Asteroid Generated Tsunamis. For
        evaluating our sampling scheme, we selected one ensemble member with
        a spatial resolution of $`300\times 300\times 300`$. Our analysis
        focuses on the water volume fraction variable, v02, which ranges
        from 0.0 (no water) to 1.0 (all water) in the simulation cell. By
        examining v02, we can visualize the resultant plume of water,
        thereby facilitating the study of ablation and ejecta as the
        asteroid impacts the water, producing a plume that spreads into the
        surrounding area and ascends into the atmosphere. Additionally, a
        small number of images were curated from the dataset documentation
        and generated from ParaView with additional variables.

## 7 Discussions

### 7.1 VizGenie: Quality Analysis

#### 7.1.1 Self-Improvement Through Expanded Visual Database

To validate the self-improving capability of VizGenie’s visual analysis
pipeline, we quantitatively assessed the system’s knowledge gain
resulting from expanding the visual database. Specifically, we compared
two scenarios for the headsq dataset: a smaller set containing 150
images (captured at 25 isovalues and 6 view angles), and an expanded set
with 300 images (captured at 50 isovalues and 6 view angles).

Our analysis showed clear improvements when using the larger image set.
Vocabulary richness significantly increased, with vocabulary size
expanding from 1606 unique words with 150 images to 2946 unique words
with 300 images, reflecting a broader and deeper representation of
dataset features. Additionally, semantic analysis revealed that mean
pairwise semantic similarity increased from 0.585 (150 images) to 0.717
(300 images). This indicates that with more images, the model achieves
greater semantic consistency and a more robust representation of
domain-specific features, which directly translates into improved
accuracy and relevance of visual question answering.

Figure
[13](#S7.F13 "Figure 13 ‣ 7.1.1 Self-Improvement Through Expanded Visual Database ‣ 7.1 VizGenie: Quality Analysis ‣ 7 Discussions ‣ VizGenie: Toward Self-Refining, Domain-Aware Workflows for Next-Generation Scientific Visualization")
illustrates these improvements, underscoring the effectiveness of
VizGenie’s asynchronous self-improvement mechanism. By autonomously
generating additional images and integrating them into its visual
knowledge base, VizGenie systematically enhances its capability for
comprehensive, insightful exploration of complex scientific datasets.

Figure 13: Quantitative analysis illustrating improvements in vocabulary
richness and semantic consistency resulting from expanding the visual
database from 150 to 300 images for the headsq dataset.

To further illustrate VizGenie’s self-improving capability, we examined
changes in predicted optimal isovalues for specific anatomical
features—namely, nose, skull, and teeth—before and after expanding the
image database from 150 to 300 images. Figure
[14](#S7.F14 "Figure 14 ‣ 7.1.1 Self-Improvement Through Expanded Visual Database ‣ 7.1 VizGenie: Quality Analysis ‣ 7 Discussions ‣ VizGenie: Toward Self-Refining, Domain-Aware Workflows for Next-Generation Scientific Visualization")
shows the isosurface similarity map (based on normalized mutual
information (MI) similarity, by Bruckner and Möller\[[4](#bib.bib4)\])
with marked optimal isovalues as returned by the VizGenie system, for
150 and 300 images. Notably, the predicted optimal isovalues aligned
more with the ideal isosurfaces as judged by a visualization expert: the
nose isovalue moved from 455 to 585 (ideal range is 650-700), skull from
1365 to 1587 (ideal range is 1550-1600), and teeth from 2730 to 2925
(ideal range is 2800-2900). These shifts underscore the system’s
enhanced understanding of the dataset, driven by its automatic,
iterative expansion of feature understanding.

![Refer to caption](2507.21124v1/figs/iso_similarity_headsq.png)

Figure 14: Isosurface similarity map and feature placement changes
resulting from expanding the visual database from 150 to 300 images for
the headsq dataset \[high-level feature areas are labeled\].

#### 7.1.2 Validation of Vision Model Fine-tuning

To assess the effectiveness of our domain-specific fine-tuning for the
Llama-3.2-Vision model (11B parameters), we conducted a comparative
analysis of caption generation before and after the fine-tuning
procedure. This qualitative analysis was performed on captions with
newly generated images from the deep-water asteroid impact dataset. This
consisted of 300 screenshots generated across 50 isovalues and 6 camera
angles for the $`v02`$ variable, the volume fraction of water. These
images were supplemented by author-captioned images from the open-source
asteroid data set release documentation \[[24](#bib.bib24)\] and
captioned ParaView visualizations generated by that author. This
supplemental sets had additional variables including the volume fraction
of asteroid ($`v03`$), the density (rho) and the temperature (tev). A
held-out set of ten ParaView visualizations were used for this analysis.
These new visualizations used the same variables and color maps as the
supplemental set of images described previously.

Our analysis revealed meaningful improvements post fine-tuning.
Pre-tuning, the model returned captions that guessed the context:
shockwave emanating from a cylindrical charge underwater, water impact
by a droplet onto a solid surface, dolphin and its jumping behavior in
the ocean, green, translucent, complex object, possibly a flower. The
most accurate sentence was: A 3D simulation of a projectile penetrating
a surface, with the projectile’s path and the surface’s deformation
visible. The model before tuning did make some accurate observations
about the color map used (green, gray, etc.) and legends. Other than
these types of purely observational remarks, there were no accurate
captions.

The fine-tuned model produced captions with increased semantic precision
and enhanced use of domain-specific vocabulary. Total vocabulary size
decreased from 4135 words before fine-tuning to a more concise and
focused 2287 words afterward. We observed substantial increases in
relevant domain-specific keyword frequencies: occurrences of "crater"
rose dramatically from 1 to 348, "asteroid" mentions increased from 0 to
1112, and "impact" rose from 38 to 1616. Conversely, general terms less
relevant to the dataset context, such as "shockwave," decreased,
demonstrating the model’s improved contextual accuracy. Additionally, we
evaluated caption stability-the consistency of descriptions generated
for identical isovalues viewed from different camera angles. After
fine-tuning, caption stability increased significantly, with the mean
inter-caption semantic similarity, Fig.
[15](#S7.F15 "Figure 15 ‣ 7.1.2 Validation of Vision Model Fine-tuning ‣ 7.1 VizGenie: Quality Analysis ‣ 7 Discussions ‣ VizGenie: Toward Self-Refining, Domain-Aware Workflows for Next-Generation Scientific Visualization"),
rising from 0.432 to 0.654 (Mann-Whitney U test, $`p<0.00001`$)

Human-in-the-loop Qualitative Analysis For a qualitative analysis of the
captions from the fine-tuned model, each separate sentence or phrase in
the overall caption was rated by the domain relevant author as TRUE or
FALSE. Compared to the effectively 0% true statements about the images
before tuning, the model improved to 39% accurate statements. While that
percentage seems low, the incorrect statements highlight the
difficulties posed for automating scientific visualization. The jargon
for the asteroid impact includes the terms: water jet, water plume, and
water vapor plume. While those terms apply to very specific and
different phenomena, the model had a tendency to use those terms
interchangeably. All color maps use were simple linear color palettes:
linear blue (rho), linear green (v02), grey (v03) and yellow-orange-red
(tev). The model often stated incorrect information about the relevant
color map such as identifying it as a log scale, when it was not. The
relevant term, transient crater, was often followed by basin, although
basin was never used in the training captions and is not a correct
description of the phenomenon.

The multi-variable aspect of some of the image data also contributed to
the tendency to produce incorrect statements. The fine-tuned model did
not always correctly identify the variable of interest. Nor could it
always identify which physical phenomenon was obscured or, conversely,
which variable was doing the obscuring.

LLM as a Judge Quantitative Analysis As a quantitative study, we used an
LLM-as-a-judge approach, prompting the LLM to do a comparison of the
out-of-the-box (OOTB) and fine-tuned models to the ground truth caption
provided by the domain relevant author. We used GPT-4o and o4-mini-high,
a reasoning model, as the judges. GPT-4o ranked the fine-tuned model
captions substantially higher with a mean of 65% compared to the OOTB
model averaging 1.7%. The o4-mini-high model was more conservative in
its opinion, with an average of 38%, still higher than the OOTB model at
20%. Details are in the supplementary material.

These improvements confirm that the fine-tuned model generates more
accurate and consistent captions and enhances the overall domain
relevance of visual question answering within VizGenie. However, these
results also show that fine-tuning for more natural language visual
phenomena such as skull and teeth is more straightforward than
fine-tuning for the more amorphous features and technical jargon of a
complex large-scale simulation dataset. There are lessons here that need
to be further explored such as how many captioned images are needed to
fine-tune the model or how to improve model understanding of the
scientific jargon, e.g., by adding additional background understanding
via domain-specific RAGs.

Figure 15: Caption stability (inter-caption similarity) comparison

fine-tuning, reflecting improved consistency and domain specificity in
generated captions.

### 7.2 Timing and Performance

Table
[1](#S7.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 7.1.2 Validation of Vision Model Fine-tuning ‣ 7.1 VizGenie: Quality Analysis ‣ 7 Discussions ‣ VizGenie: Toward Self-Refining, Domain-Aware Workflows for Next-Generation Scientific Visualization")
summarizes the performance metrics for various visualization tasks
executed by different LLM models within VizGenie. Due to the general
stochasticity of the LLMs, these numbers are collected by averaging over
five executions of the same prompts. During this two step evaluation,
first we checked if the LLMs are generating executable code and then, if
the code executes and produces output, we checked if the user
specifications were correctly incorporated. User specifications include
visualization choice (e.g., volume rendering, isosurface), visualization
parameters (e.g., choice of isovalue, colormaps, background color). We
observe that code generation tasks, such as volume rendering and
isosurface creation, typically require more processing time
(approximately 15 to 23 seconds), whereas simpler operations via
preexisting tools like slicing and histogram generation complete
significantly faster (about 2 to 4 seconds). Notably, the gpt-4o and
o3-mini models generally produce valid and robust outputs (validity
scores close to 1), though the smaller (and cheaper) model variants
(gpt-4o-mini) occasionally compromise validity but are generally
slightly faster. For using preexisting tools via agentic reasoning, the
gpt-4o model provides the highest quality in reasonable interaction
time. These results highlight a trade-off between model complexity,
validity, and response time, underscoring the importance of model
selection tailored to task complexity within an interactive
visualization workflow.

### 7.3 User Feedback

The authors represent broad expertise from physics, HPC, visualization,
and AI/ML. Various authors contributed labeled input to the framework
and user feedback on the interface and case studies. Most of the authors
providing feedback were regular users of LLMs in their daily work. As
early users of the framework, the authors explored various prompts using
the chat interface and provided feedback on additional features that
would be helpful in the tool. The natural language-based feature
exploration and simplicity of the user interface were considered
strengths by these early users. The interactive nature of the agent,
particularly in suggesting next queries was also well-received. The VQA
aspect was highly rated although early users were somewhat disappointed
when the VQA system did not yield the exact answer. Early users also
noted that at times their prompts were misinterpreted by the agent/LLMs.
One primary reason was that vocabulary differs across domains. Keywords
such as "show", "explore", "visualize" can mean different operations
based on the user and their expertise/understanding of the problem.
These early use cases informed the development and evolution of
VizGenie.

Iterative Improvements Driven by User Feedback: Early interactions with
domain experts and initial users highlighted the need for more accurate
and domain-specific visual interpretations, as generic vision models
frequently produced irrelevant or misleading descriptions of complex
scientific visualizations. In response to this critical feedback, we
implemented targeted fine-tuning of the vision models (specifically
Llama-Vision) using domain-specific datasets. This iterative enhancement
significantly improved the semantic precision, caption stability, and
domain relevance of VizGenie’s VQA capability, directly addressing
user-identified limitations. Despite the improvements due to
fine-tuning, since we use LLM-based operators to search for features in
the feature database, we sometimes get unexpected results and must
resubmit the prompt to regenerate answers. We would like to address in
our future work.

## 8 Limitations and Future Work

Despite its promising performance and innovative design, VizGenie has
several limitations that provide avenues for future research. The
reliance on multiple large language models (LLMs) introduces latency and
computational overhead, potentially affecting real-time responsiveness
with large datasets or complex queries. Moreover, the accuracy and
reproducibility of dynamically generated modules and incremental code
modifications depend significantly on LLM outputs, which may
occasionally contain errors, variability, or biases originating from
training data. The current domain-specific fine-tuning approach is
manually initiated, limiting seamless generalization across different
scientific domains. Additionally, the retrieval-augmented generation
(RAG) mechanism is presently limited, restricting its ability to
leverage fully contextual learning for extensive validation or optimal
parameter suggestions. Further, we currently limit the pipeline to VTK
for reading and visualizing the data, directing the LLMs to generate
only VTK code. Using VTK keeps VizGenie lightweight during this early
development process. In the future, we could consider merging VizGenie
capabilities with visualization tools such as ParaView or VisIt.

Future research includes developing more efficient, scalable LLM
architectures, such as model distillation and quantization, to reduce
latency without compromising output quality. We aim to automate
domain-specific fine-tuning through continuous learning frameworks,
improving VizGenie’s adaptability across diverse scientific contexts and
data types. Advanced retrieval-augmented generation methods
incorporating sophisticated vector databases and embedding-based
retrieval will also be explored to provide richer contextual insights
and reduce manual interventions. Beyond VTK functionalities, we will
prototype more sophisticated multi-agent systems to auto-analyze and
generate new data readers and user-directed non-VTK visualizations.

We will investigate emerging multi-modal LLMs and generative diffusion
models to expand visualization capabilities, with the goal of automated
novel visualization generation directly from user queries. Extensive
user studies are needed along with rigorous quantitative evaluations
across diverse real-world datasets. These evaluations will guide
VizGenie’s iterative refinement, ensuring its sustained relevance and
effectiveness within high-performance computing scientific visualization
workflows.
